marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q001.takeaway: Sartorius is the longest muscle in the body, running obliquely from ASIS to the medial proximal tibia.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q001.displayText:
Sartorius is the longest muscle in the body, running obliquely from ASIS to the medial proximal tibia.

The sartorius muscle is the longest muscle in the body.

It originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and inserts into the superior aspect of the medial surface of the tibial shaft near the tibial tuberosity, joining gracilis and semitendinosus at the pes anserinus.

It flexes and laterally rotates the hip joint and flexes the knee, and is innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, and L4).
emphasis: Sartorius is the longest muscle in the body, running obliquely from ASIS to the medial proximal tibia

rationales.a: Gracilis is a long medial-thigh muscle, but it is shorter than sartorius.
rationales.c: Adductor longus is a triangular medial-thigh muscle, not the body's longest muscle.
rationales.d: Biceps femoris is a posterior-thigh hamstring with a shorter course than sartorius.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q002.takeaway: Gluteus maximus inserts mainly into the iliotibial tract and also the gluteal tuberosity.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q002.displayText:
Gluteus maximus inserts mainly into the iliotibial tract and also the gluteal tuberosity.

The gluteus maximus muscle is attached to the iliotibial tract of the fascia lata.

Origin: posterior aspect of dorsal ilium posterior to posterior gluteal line; posterior superior iliac spine; posterior aspect of sacrum and coccyx; sacrotuberous ligament.

Insertion: mainly into fascia lata at the iliotibial band and also the gluteal tuberosity on the posterior femoral surface.

Actions: major extensor of hip joint; lateral rotation of hip joint; active in powerful abduction of thigh.

Arterial supply: inferior and superior gluteal arteries and first perforating branch of profunda femoris artery. Nerve supply: inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1 and S2).
emphasis: Gluteus maximus inserts mainly into the iliotibial tract and also the gluteal tuberosity

rationales.a: Gluteus medius/minimus and short rotators insert around the greater trochanter; gluteus maximus inserts chiefly on IT tract and gluteal tuberosity.
rationales.b: Iliopsoas inserts on the lesser trochanter, not gluteus maximus.
rationales.d: The spiral line receives muscle attachments but is not the principal gluteus maximus insertion.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q003.takeaway: Gluteus medius (label 2) abducts and stabilizes the pelvis during single-leg stance; weakness produces a Trendelenburg-type gait.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q003.displayText:
Gluteus medius (label 2) abducts and stabilizes the pelvis during single-leg stance; weakness produces a Trendelenburg-type gait.

The structure involved in causing lurching gait in the child is gluteus medius, marked as 2.

Gluteus medius originates from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines and inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

Gluteus medius and minimus are powerful abductors of the hip joint. When the leg on one side is lifted, the gluteus medius and minimus on the opposite supported side exert traction on the hip bone and raise the pelvis slightly on the unsupported side, helping maintain the trunk upright.

These actions are affected by superior gluteal nerve injury, fracture of the neck of femur, or loss of normal shaft angulation. With paralysis, the pelvis sinks on the unsupported normal side when standing on the affected limb, producing a positive Trendelenburg sign and a characteristic lurch toward the affected side with contralateral pelvic drop.

Other options described by the source: 1 is gluteus maximus; 3 is piriformis; 4 is the sciatic nerve.
emphasis: Gluteus medius (label 2) abducts and stabilizes the pelvis during single-leg stance; weakness produces a Trendelenburg-type gait

rationales.a: Label 1 is not the gluteus medius specified by the source key; the weak hip abductor on the stance side causes contralateral pelvic drop.
rationales.c: Label 3 is a different marked structure; the gait sign localizes to gluteus medius, label 2.
rationales.d: Label 4 does not identify the abductor in the source figure; gluteus medius is the relevant pelvic stabilizer.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q004.takeaway: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus; denervation weakens powerful hip extension and can cause a gluteus-maximus lurch.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q004.displayText:
The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus; denervation weakens powerful hip extension and can cause a gluteus-maximus lurch.

In the given clinical scenario, the inferior gluteal nerve is likely to be injured.

The gluteus maximus is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve. Injury causes muscle atrophy and weakness of thigh extension, producing a gluteus maximus lurch. The muscle may be tested by extension of the hip against resistance in the supine or prone position.
emphasis: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus; denervation weakens powerful hip extension and can cause a gluteus-maximus lurch

rationales.a: The sciatic nerve passes deep to gluteus maximus and supplies posterior-thigh muscles, not gluteus maximus itself.
rationales.b: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius/minimus and tensor fasciae latae, not gluteus maximus.
rationales.d: The femoral nerve supplies anterior-thigh muscles and does not innervate gluteus maximus.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q005.takeaway: The gluteal tuberosity receives gluteus maximus, whose hip actions include extension and lateral rotation.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q005.displayText:
The gluteal tuberosity receives gluteus maximus, whose hip actions include extension and lateral rotation.

The image shows the posterior surface of the femur. The marked area is the gluteal tuberosity, to which gluteus maximus is attached; gluteus maximus causes extension and lateral rotation at the hip joint.

The proximal femur consists of the head, neck and greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is anterior at the neck-shaft junction and the intertrochanteric crest is posterior. The shaft includes linea aspera, gluteal tuberosity and pectineal line. The distal femur includes medial and lateral condyles, intercondylar fossa and patellar surface.

Gluteus maximus origin, insertion, action, arterial supply and nerve supply are reiterated in the source: insertion mainly into the iliotibial band with additional insertion into gluteal tuberosity; major hip extension and lateral rotation; powerful abduction; inferior gluteal nerve supply.
emphasis: The gluteal tuberosity receives gluteus maximus, whose hip actions include extension and lateral rotation

rationales.a: Abduction with external rotation is not the principal combined action of gluteus maximus at the hip.
rationales.c: Adduction can be assisted by lower gluteus maximus fibers, but extension and lateral rotation are the source-keyed actions.
rationales.d: Hip flexion is opposite the main extension action of gluteus maximus.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q006.takeaway: Gluteus medius inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter and abducts the hip.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q006.displayText:
Gluteus medius inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter and abducts the hip.

Gluteus medius is attached to the lateral surface of the greater trochanter.

The greater trochanter is a large quadrangular projection at the neck-shaft junction. Muscles inserted on it include gluteus minimus, gluteus medius, piriformis, and the common tendon of obturator internus and gemelli.

The lesser trochanter is conical and posteromedial; iliacus and psoas major insert on it. The source notes that the greater trochanter lies inferior to the midpoint of the iliac crest and at the level of the horizontal plane through the pubic tubercle.
emphasis: Gluteus medius inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter and abducts the hip

rationales.a: Gluteus minimus inserts on the anterior rather than the lateral surface of the greater trochanter.
rationales.c: Gluteus maximus inserts on the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity, not the greater trochanter's lateral surface.
rationales.d: Piriformis inserts near the superior border of the greater trochanter, not its lateral surface.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q007.takeaway: Tensor fasciae latae inserts into the iliotibial tract, which continues distally to Gerdy's tubercle.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q007.displayText:
Tensor fasciae latae inserts into the iliotibial tract, which continues distally to Gerdy's tubercle.

The iliotibial tract receives the insertion of tensor fasciae latae.

The iliotibial tract is a modification of the deep fascia of the thigh. Its proximal end gives attachment to tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus, and its distal end attaches to Gerdy’s tubercle on the lateral tibial condyle.
emphasis: Tensor fasciae latae inserts into the iliotibial tract, which continues distally to Gerdy's tubercle

rationales.a: Gluteus minimus inserts on the greater trochanter and does not join the iliotibial tract.
rationales.b: Gluteus medius inserts on the greater trochanter rather than into the IT tract.
rationales.d: Sartorius inserts at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia, not into the IT tract.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q008.takeaway: Gluteus medius is a powerful hip abductor and helps keep the pelvis level during gait.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q008.displayText:
Gluteus medius is a powerful hip abductor and helps keep the pelvis level during gait.

The powerful abductor of the hip joint is gluteus medius.

Abduction is assisted by gluteus minimus, tensor fascia lata, piriformis and sartorius.

Adduction is mainly caused by adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus and gracilis. Flexion is caused by psoas major, iliacus and rectus femoris and assisted by pectineus, tensor fascia lata and sartorius. Extension is caused by gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus and adductor magnus, assisted by posterior fibres of gluteus medius.
emphasis: Gluteus medius is a powerful hip abductor and helps keep the pelvis level during gait

rationales.a: Gluteus maximus is primarily a hip extensor and lateral rotator, not the principal abductor.
rationales.b: Obturator internus is a short lateral rotator of the extended hip, not a powerful abductor.
rationales.c: Quadratus femoris laterally rotates the hip; it is not a principal abductor.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q009.takeaway: Gluteus maximus is a powerful lateral rotator of the hip; gluteus medius/minimus and tensor fasciae latae contribute to medial rotation.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q009.displayText:
Gluteus maximus is a powerful lateral rotator of the hip; gluteus medius/minimus and tensor fasciae latae contribute to medial rotation.

External rotation of the hip joint is caused by gluteus maximus, obturator internus, superior and inferior gemelli, quadratus femoris and piriformis, assisted by obturator externus and sartorius.

Internal rotation is caused by gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fascia lata and adductor muscles.
emphasis: Gluteus maximus is a powerful lateral rotator of the hip; gluteus medius/minimus and tensor fasciae latae contribute to medial rotation

rationales.a: Gluteus medius helps medially rotate the hip, especially through its anterior fibers.
rationales.c: Tensor fasciae latae flexes and medially rotates the hip while tensioning the IT tract.
rationales.d: Adductor longus adducts and can assist medial rotation, rather than being the listed external rotator.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q010.takeaway: The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings through tibial and common fibular divisions; most posterior-thigh muscles are innervated by it.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q010.displayText:
The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings through tibial and common fibular divisions; most posterior-thigh muscles are innervated by it.

The posterior femoral muscles (hamstrings) are innervated by the sciatic nerve.

Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and the long head of biceps femoris are innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1 and S2). The short head of biceps femoris is innervated by the common peroneal division of the sciatic nerve.
emphasis: The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings through tibial and common fibular divisions; most posterior-thigh muscles are innervated by it

rationales.a: The femoral nerve innervates anterior-thigh muscles, particularly quadriceps, rather than the hamstrings.
rationales.b: The obturator nerve primarily supplies medial-thigh adductors, not the posterior hamstrings.
rationales.d: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus; it is not the nerve to posterior femoral muscles.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q011.takeaway: The short head of biceps femoris arises from the femur, not the ischial tuberosity; the other listed muscles have ischial origins.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q011.displayText:
The short head of biceps femoris arises from the femur, not the ischial tuberosity; the other listed muscles have ischial origins.

The short head of biceps femoris is not attached to the ischial tuberosity. It attaches to the lateral lip of linea aspera, lateral supracondylar ridge of the femur and lateral intermuscular septum of the thigh.

The ischial tuberosity has upper and lower areas. The upper area is subdivided into a superolateral part for semimembranosus and an inferomedial part for the long head of biceps femoris and semitendinosus. The lower area is divided by an irregular vertical ridge; the larger lateral area is for adductor magnus and the smaller medial area is covered by adipose tissue and usually contains the sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus.
emphasis: The short head of biceps femoris arises from the femur, not the ischial tuberosity; the other listed muscles have ischial origins

rationales.a: Semimembranosus arises from the ischial tuberosity and is a hamstring muscle.
rationales.b: Semitendinosus arises from the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the pes anserinus.
rationales.d: The hamstring part of adductor magnus arises from the ischial tuberosity, unlike the short head of biceps.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q012.takeaway: Piriformis syndrome commonly involves sciatic nerve irritation where the nerve passes near or below piriformis.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q012.displayText:
Piriformis syndrome commonly involves sciatic nerve irritation where the nerve passes near or below piriformis.

The clinical features are suggestive of piriformis syndrome due to entrapment of the sciatic nerve.

It can be triggered by prolonged sitting, running, climbing stairs or firm pressure over piriformis. Early symptoms include pain, tingling or numbness in the buttocks; later, severe pain may extend down the course of the sciatic nerve.
emphasis: Piriformis syndrome commonly involves sciatic nerve irritation where the nerve passes near or below piriformis

rationales.a: The obturator nerve exits through the obturator canal to the medial thigh, not through the greater sciatic foramen by piriformis.
rationales.b: The superior gluteal nerve exits above piriformis and supplies abductors; it is not the nerve typically entrapped in piriformis syndrome.
rationales.c: The inferior gluteal nerve exits below piriformis to supply gluteus maximus; the sciatic nerve is the classic entrapment.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q013.takeaway: Sartorius is not a hamstring; the hamstrings are semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris (long head).
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q013.displayText:
Sartorius is not a hamstring; the hamstrings are semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris (long head).

Sartorius is not part of the hamstring muscles.

Hamstrings are in the posterior compartment of the thigh and include semimembranosus, semitendinosus and biceps femoris. They flex the knee and extend the hip. Semimembranosus and semitendinosus medially rotate the hip and knee, whereas biceps femoris laterally rotates them.
emphasis: Sartorius is not a hamstring; the hamstrings are semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris (long head)

rationales.a: Biceps femoris long head is a hamstring and arises from the ischial tuberosity.
rationales.c: Semitendinosus is a hamstring that extends the hip and flexes the knee.
rationales.d: Semimembranosus is a hamstring muscle of the posterior thigh.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q014.takeaway: Gracilis belongs to the medial thigh compartment; vasti and rectus femoris belong to the anterior compartment.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q014.displayText:
Gracilis belongs to the medial thigh compartment; vasti and rectus femoris belong to the anterior compartment.

Gracilis belongs to the medial compartment of the thigh.

Anterior-compartment muscles listed by the source are sartorius, rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius and articularis genus.

The source notes that adductor longus and pectineus are sometimes considered part of both anterior and medial compartments.
emphasis: Gracilis belongs to the medial thigh compartment; vasti and rectus femoris belong to the anterior compartment

rationales.a: Vastus lateralis is part of the quadriceps in the anterior compartment.
rationales.b: Rectus femoris is an anterior-compartment quadriceps muscle.
rationales.c: Vastus medialis is part of the anterior-compartment quadriceps.
